full_judgment: 11. An amendment in the plaint is allowed for determining the real question in controversy between the parties and once an amendment of the plaint is allowed the amendment will relate back to the date of the institution of the suit and will be operative from that date. The defendants did not challenge the amendment in the plaint and the Court of appeal below, in the premises, erred in law in disputing the plaintiffs' claim only because those facts were not pleaded in the original plaint. The Court of appeal below fell in an error in failing to appreciate that no particular form is necessary in executing a will. It is sufficient if it contains the testamentary wishes of the deceased; the reference in this connection is sections 377 and 378 of the Hindu Law. A will is the legal declaration of the intention of a testator with respect to his property which he desires to be carried into effect after his death. Primarily, the words of the will are to be considered. They convey the expression of the stator's wishes. In Exhibit 7 the testator stated that on his demise, his wife Feli and nephew Kailash would enjoy his property in /4/ and /12/ annas share respectively and that on the death of his wife, Kailash would get her share as well. It is a registered instrument and executed on 17th February, 1913, more than 86 years prior to its filing in Court on 23rd November, 1999 by the plaintiffs from their custody claiming that Kailash got Ketu's share in the khatian on the strength of this will. It being a document of more than 30 years old produced from the proper custody, the Court may presume that (a) the signature and every other part of it which purports to be in the handwriting of the scribe is in that person's' handwriting, (b) the will was executed by Ketu, and (c) the will was attested by the persons by whom it purported to have been attested under section 90 of the Evidence Act. There is also presumption that the will was prepared at the time it was purported to have been prepared. The Court of appeal below has totally ignored this legal aspect of the matter while considering the will, Exhibit 7.
